## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The register's entry is a specification, and specifications are written before things are built.**

Every clause of it is accurate as a description of the design. There were smaller electric motors across the wing leading edge acting as a high lift device. There were larger motors mounted on each wing tip for cruise. **The wing was designed for that configuration, and this article has spent several sections showing how tightly it was designed for it.**

**What the entry cannot record is readiness.** A designation register records what a vehicle is for. It has no column for whether the parts exist at the maturity the plan assumed, and that is the quantity on which this programme turned.

**The length of the entry is evidence of the same thing.** The X-57 has the most detailed mission statement of any X designation because by 2016 the architecture was fully worked out on paper. **The confidence that produced a 328 character specification is the same confidence that produced a technology readiness assessment describing an integration task.**

## The Source Base

**The research survey behind this article holds 2,081 records, drawn from Crossref, NASA's Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 169 are report primaries, being 8.1 percent, by the rule set out under The Definition of Primary.

### A Programme's Own Index Cannot Be Searched, Only Read

**NASA publishes a page listing the X-57 programme's technical output.** It carries sixty-three entries, of which sixty-one resolve against the report server and the other two carry metadata too thin to identify \[[X-57 Technical Papers, NASA Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate][ref_nasa_x57_papers]\].

**The report server's search interface cannot reach that output.** A direct query for the designation reports seventy-four matching records and returns ten. Asking for a hundred returns ten. **Asking for the eleventh onward, by offset, returns the same ten again**, at every offset from ten to seventy. The offset is ignored by the endpoint, so the remaining sixty-four records cannot be reached by that interface at all. **A programme's own published index must be read. It cannot be searched.**

**60 of the 2,081 research records come from that list**, which NASA maintains as a page of technical papers rather than as a bibliography inside any one report \[[X-57 Technical Papers, NASA Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate][ref_nasa_x57_papers]\].

### The Age of the Literature

**The median year of the research records is 2020.** 1,374 of the 1,960 that carry a year, being 70 percent, were published in 2015 or later, and 103 predate 1980. **The youngest clusters are the battery, with a median year of 2024, cooling at 2023 and distributed electric propulsion at 2022, and the oldest is measurement, at 1999**, so the literature this aeroplane draws on is newest where its energy store and its architecture are.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on NASA's Technical Reports Server or it carries a Defense Technical Information Center identifier. **169 of the 2,081 research records are report primaries under that rule**, being 8.1 percent. The rule measures where a document is hosted rather than what it is, so a programme paper published only by the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics counts as conference literature, while a report-server copy of a secondary study counts as a report.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures in this survey.** Each count below is the number of research records whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---:|
| the stall rule for propulsion used as a high-lift device | minimum steady flight speed, stall speed, stalling speed, stall requirement together with powered, propeller, propulsion, blown, blowing, slipstream, thrust | 0 |
| folding propeller blades | folding, foldable, folded together with propeller, blade | 1 |
| power electronics under vibration | vibration, vibratory together with inverter, power module, power electronics, motor controller, MOSFET, converter, gate driver | 0 |
| shoot-through in a half bridge | shoot through, cross conduction | 0 |
| the thermal interface between a switch and its heat sink | thermal interface, gap pad, thermal pad, interface material | 0 |
| qualifying an electric motor for flight | motor, electric machine, electric engine, propulsion unit, electric or electrified propulsion together with qualification, certification, airworthiness, Part 33, endurance test, flightworthy, specification | 12 |
| technology readiness assessment | technology readiness, readiness level, readiness assessment | 6 |

**The stall rule that shaped the high-lift system has no literature here.** No title joins a stall speed term to a powered, blown or propeller term, so the reading of the stall rule reported above rests on the flight performance report and the regulation alone.

**The folding propeller is the X-57's own subject.** The one title that names a folding blade is the programme's analysis of folding conformal blade designs.

**The three failure mechanisms that stopped the controllers are absent from the survey's titles.** No title joins vibration to an inverter, a power module or a controller, none names shoot-through, and none names the thermal interface between a switch and its heat sink. Crossref nonetheless holds a literature on thermal interface materials for power modules and on shoot-through in inverters, so the absence marks the edge of this survey rather than of power electronics, and the failure history in this article rests on the programme's own documents.

**Qualifying an electric motor for flight is, in this survey, a literature of specifications.** Of the 12 titles, 7 are ASTM International specifications for electric propulsion units, electric engines, aircraft electric propulsion systems and the electrical systems of electric aircraft, and the other 5 concern airworthiness, certification and the qualification of the SCEPTOR power system for crewed flight testing. Whether any of the specifications would have served as the flight qualification standard that the traction power account found lacking is not something a title can show.

**The readiness assessment at the root of the programme's difficulty has a small literature, and none of it names an aircraft.** The 6 titles concern defence acquisition, software and space systems, so the lesson this article draws from the X-57's readiness assessment stands on the programme's own lessons learned reports.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is the X-57 and the Tecnam P2006T it was built from, named explicitly, together with the blown wing, the propellers, the electric machinery and the switching devices that drive it, the battery, the drag and lift of the small wing, the sizing, certification and testing of such an aeroplane, and the atmosphere in which it flies. The atmosphere is admitted as a subject rather than a setting, because the whole architecture exists to raise the dynamic pressure over the wing by means other than flying faster.

**A title on a flight vehicle is admitted only when its subject is one that this article reasons with, unless the title names the X-57 or the Tecnam P2006T.** Rotorcraft, tiltrotors, multirotors, airships and other vertical takeoff aircraft are excluded where the title concerns the vehicle itself, its hover, transition, control, sizing or certification, rather than its battery, motors, cooling, propellers or the interaction of its propellers with a wing. Joined wings and flying wings are excluded, and so are jet transports and fighters, their design, aerodynamics, engines, flight test and control, where the title's subject is not electric or propeller propulsion, high lift, induced drag or the high aspect ratio wing itself. So are general aeronautical subjects that the argument never uses, among them delta and low aspect ratio wings, vortex lift, flapping and heaving wings, dynamic stall, the drag of bluff bodies, afterbodies and stores, the noise of anything other than distributed or electric propulsion, avionics and flight control computers, the health monitoring of conventional engines and airframes, landing gear, aviation fuels, aircraft materials, maintenance and operations, the airworthiness of unmanned aircraft and of equipment the argument never uses, and the cost, emissions and climate effects of aviation. The wind shear, structural loads and control laws of powered-lift transports are excluded as well, since only the blowing that produces their lift bears on this wing. Semiconductor devices other than power switches, cryogenic coolers, capacitors and dielectrics, whose energy density is another homonym, and the stationary storage of the electrical grid fall outside the survey, and so do trade newsletter items, which report news rather than research.

**Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record whose title shares only such a word is excluded.** The aeroplane is named after James Clerk Maxwell \[[James Clerk Maxwell][ref_maxwell]\], whose surname is also attached to a set of equations, a velocity distribution, a viscoelastic material model and a polarization theory \[[Maxwell's Equations][ref_maxwell_equations]\] \[[Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution][ref_maxwell_distribution]\], so the Love numbers of a generalized Maxwell sphere, membrane polarization in shaly sands and the teaching of the Maxwell distribution fall outside the survey. Energy density also names explosives and strain energy, silicon carbide also names armour and structural ceramics, drag reduction also names polymer and particle additives in liquids and the shapes of animals and plants, wing loading also names bats, birds and insects, low power also names digital electronics, aspect ratio also names microfabrication and seismic bearings, and power density also names radar, antennas and ocean waves. Electric propulsion also names the ion, Hall, arc and plasma thrusters of spacecraft, so that literature, its conferences and its programme reviews included, falls outside the survey, and so do marine propellers, rudders and ship drives, wind and tidal turbines, and road vehicles where the title concerns driving range, charging or fleets rather than a battery, motor or inverter. Flow in the transonic and supersonic regimes is excluded as well, because this aeroplane cruises at 150 knots. Correction, erratum, corrigendum and withdrawal notices, retracted papers and supplementary-material records are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. Reviews of books and reference and definition entries are excluded for the same reason, since neither reports research, and so are unsigned news items, the listing of a document in an abstract journal, and the bare text of a resolution.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** 61 titles on the battery, motor, inverter or cooling of a road vehicle are kept, because the cell, the pack and the drive are the same physics as the X-57's. Records on the rotors of electrical machines are kept, because here the electrical machine is the subject, and one of this article's own primary documents is a finite element electromagnetic model of a permanent magnet synchronous cruise motor \[[Marrufo and Kloesel 2019][research_x57_cruise_motor_electromagnetic]\]. Domain-free studies of turbulent drag reduction and of actuator disc theory are kept, because neither names an application outside flight. Records on the noise of distributed propulsion are kept, because distributed propulsion is the register's own subject. Records on hybrid electric, turbo-electric, fuel cell and hydrogen aircraft are kept as well, because their machines, power electronics and energy sums are the X-57's subjects. Five book chapters titled only General Aviation are kept, since a title that short cannot be placed more exactly. The last cluster admits a title only when it passes the rule above and names the subject of no other cluster, and a title that names electric propulsion without an application is kept there only when it was published in 2000 or later, because before then the phrase meant the propulsion of spacecraft.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only. Where one document is deposited twice, as a report-server copy and a published version or as a preprint and its journal version, one record is kept.

## Epistemic State

**Facts.** The register's wording and the counts taken across its 539 rows, the geometry, masses, powers and energies attributed to the flight performance report and the traction power documents, the battery figures attributed to the 2018 battery account, the flight-test plan, the controller and motor histories attributed to the traction power papers, the schedule attributed to the systems engineering and lessons learned reports, and the failure modes attributed to the inverter deck, are quoted from those documents, and every arithmetic relation stated here has been recomputed rather than repeated. The register is counted in a copy later than this article's date, and the counts that differ in the version current on that date are stated where the empty engines cell is discussed \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, 11 August 2025][ref_mds_addendum_2025]\].

**Inference.** That the length of the register entry reflects the maturity of the paper design is an inference. It is consistent with the entry being a specification rather than a purpose clause, and with the readiness assessment made in the same period, but the register does not say why the entry is long.

**Assumptions.** The propulsive efficiency of 75 percent used in the blowing estimates and the range bound is assumed here and stated by no source. The stall-speed lift coefficients use sea level standard density at 1,361 kilograms and treat the tabulated calibrated airspeeds as equivalent airspeeds. The slipstream model that credits a fraction of the span with a uniform velocity increase is a simplification made here, not the designers' model, and the high-lift propeller diameter is rounded to 1.9 feet in it.

**Inference.** That the full configuration would have come within reach of the goal of five times lower energy use rests on multiplying estimates made at different conditions.

**Hypothesis.** That the buy-American direction is the proximate cause of the readiness mismatch is close to what the lessons learned report says but slightly stronger than it. **The report's position is that the project may have benefitted from reassessing the readiness of American components and that the actual readiness proved significantly lower.** \[[Maliska et al. 2024][research_x57_lessons_learned]\] It does not assert that the direction caused the mismatch, and neither does this article.

**Unresolved.** The high-lift motor power is given as 12.6 kilowatts by the flight performance report and as 10.5 kilowatts by NASA's X-57 page \[[X-57 Maxwell Overview, NASA][ref_nasa_x57]\]. This article uses the report's figure and records the disagreement. The same NASA page gives the battery as 69.1 kilowatt hours, 47 of them usable, in 860 pounds \[[X-57 Maxwell Overview, NASA][ref_nasa_x57]\], which is 80 watt hours per pound, and that is the specific energy secondary sources quote \[[NASA X-57 Maxwell][ref_x57_wikipedia]\]. The nominal cell energy rebuilt here from the battery account's cell, 55.3 kilowatt hours, gives 64 over the same 860 pounds and the effective 47 kilowatt hours gives 55, so NASA's page and the battery account disagree on the stored energy, 69.1 against 55.3 kilowatt hours, and neither document reconciles the two. The 2018 battery account also gives sixteen modules of 51 pounds, which is 816 pounds against the 860 it states for the battery, and the remainder is not itemised. The as-built usable energy of 23 kilowatt hours a pack is lower than the 2018 effective figure, and the relations in this article use the 2018 figure. NASA's X-57 page gives each cruise motor with its propeller as 117 pounds in its specification table and as about 57 pounds in its text \[[X-57 Maxwell Overview, NASA][ref_nasa_x57]\]. The motor's design masses and the propeller budget support the table, and the power density comparison uses it. That the 57 is the Rotax's mass in kilograms under the wrong unit is an inference, and the page does not say so.

## Out of Scope

**Whether battery aviation is a good idea is out of scope.** This article computes what this aeroplane's numbers were and does not extrapolate them to a technology.

**The certification consequences are argued here only where they shaped the aeroplane**, in the stall rule for propellers used as a high-lift device. The programme published a certification gap analysis and an airworthiness validation plan \[[Schlickenmaier et al. 2019b][research_x57_certification_gap_analysis]\] \[[Schlickenmaier et al. 2023][research_x57_airworthiness_validation_plan]\], and what a normal category aeroplane has to prove is written down \[[14 CFR Part 23, Airworthiness Standards for Normal Category Aeroplanes][ref_part23]\]. Those belong to a different article, and the programme's own view of what it left behind is published \[[X-57 Project Creates Paths Toward Electric Aviation, NASA][ref_nasa_x57_paths]\].

## Conclusion

**The register gave this aeroplane the most detailed entry of any X designation, and the aeroplane never flew.**

The entry is not wrong. **The wing was designed optimally for the electric motor configuration**, and the design is tight enough that its parts can only be understood together. The wing was cut to 42 percent of its area to reduce drag in cruise. That made it unable to land, so twelve propellers were put along its leading edge to blow it. Those propellers add wetted area, so the parasite saving fell from 58 percent to 18. The span came down as the aspect ratio went up, so the induced drag rose by 32 percent. **The cruise propellers went to the wingtips because after all of that the configuration needed the vortex energy back.**

**The blowing closes on the installed power only because the propellers were never asked for the full factor.** Treated as ideal discs, they could not have supplied a factor of 2.38 once any real efficiency is allowed. The flapped small wing supplies a factor of 1.51 by itself and the propellers the remaining 1.58, and on that division the design thrust and the installed power both leave margin. **That is a computation on predictions, not a result from flight**, and the aeroplane never flew to test it.

**And underneath every one of those decisions is a battery carrying a hundredth of the energy per kilogram of the fuel it replaced**, giving back a factor of three in drivetrain efficiency and leaving a factor of thirty-three to be found somewhere in the aerodynamics.

**None of that is what stopped it.** The transistors in the motor controllers failed under vibration, failed under heat, and failed when the software commanded both halves of a bridge to conduct at once, and the controllers had to be redesigned. The first battery burned in its propagation test and had to be redesigned. The cruise motors, after years of operational workarounds, were found to need a stator redesign that the remaining time and money could not buy. **The programme had been scoped on the assumption that those parts could be bought rather than developed**, and the assessment that produced that assumption was never repeated after the sourcing direction that invalidated it.

**The aeroplane was not shown to be impossible.** The cruise motors as then configured were judged an unacceptable risk for flight, and the team was working toward a design review for a modified motor when the money and the schedule ran out. **What the sources record is a programme that ran out of both, not a machine that could not be built.**

**A designation register has a column for the contractor, the sponsor, the engines and the mission, and for this row the engines column is empty.** That blank turned out to mean nothing, since ninety-four rows share it. **The blank that would have mattered is the one no register has**, a column for whether the parts exist yet at the maturity the plan assumed.

**The X-57's entry is the longest in its class because the design was finished.** The design being finished is not the same as the parts being ready, and a register can record only the first.

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 57 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 57, 44 are established and 13 are bespoke.
Areas are in square metres, speeds inside the equations in metres per second although the stall speeds are quoted in knots, powers in kilowatts, energies in kilowatt hours, specific energies in watt hours per kilogram, ranges in kilometres and torque in newton metres, and $e$ is the span efficiency while $e_b$ and $e_f$ are the specific energies of the battery and the fuel, with Roman numerals marking the Mod I to Mod IV configurations.

**Equation 1, Ratio of Mod III to Original Wing Area.**
The reported wing areas give a Mod III wing of 42 percent of the area of the wing it replaced.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{S_1}{S_0} = \frac{6.19}{14.76} = 0.419
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Wing Loading.**
The wing loading is the weight a wing must carry per unit of its own area.

$$
\frac{W}{S} \quad\text{is what a wing must carry per unit of its own area}
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Ratio of Wing Loadings at Equal Mass.**
At the same mass the wing loading rises by the reciprocal of the area ratio, a factor of 2.38.

$$
\frac{(W/S)_1}{(W/S)_0} = \frac{S_0}{S_1} = 2.38
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Lift Equation.**
Lift is the dynamic pressure times the wing area times the lift coefficient.
[Lift Coefficient][ref_lift_coefficient]

$$
L = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} S\, C_L
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Stall Speed.**
The stall speed is set by the wing loading, the air density and the maximum lift coefficient.
[Wing Loading][ref_wing_loading]
[Stall, Fluid Dynamics][ref_stall_speed]
[Lift Coefficient][ref_lift_coefficient]

$$
V_s = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\rho}\,\frac{W}{S}\,\frac{1}{C_{L,max}}}
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Dynamic Pressure in a Propeller Slipstream.**
A propeller ahead of a wing adds a velocity increment that raises the local dynamic pressure above the free-stream value.
[Dynamic Pressure][ref_dynamic_pressure]

$$
q_w = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,(V + \Delta V)^{2} \;>\; \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}
\tag{6}
$$

*Equation 7, Bespoke Blown Span Fraction.*
The article takes each slipstream to cover one propeller diameter of span, with the diameter rounded to 1.9 feet, so that twelve propellers blow about seventy percent of the span.
[Borer and Patterson][research_x57_high_lift_control_schedule]

$$
f = \frac{12\,d}{b_1} = \frac{6.95}{9.94} = 0.70
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Total High-Lift Propeller Disc Area.**
The twelve discs of the rounded diameter give a total disc area of 3.16 square metres.

$$
A_h = 12\,\frac{\pi d^{2}}{4} = 3.16
\tag{8}
$$

*Equation 9, Bespoke Slipstream Lift Multiple.*
The article models the blown fraction as seeing a uniformly increased velocity at unchanged lift coefficient and the rest the free stream, and sets the weighted lift multiple equal to the area ratio.

$$
f\,(1+x)^{2} + (1-f) = \frac{S_0}{S_1}
\tag{9}
$$

*Equation 10, Bespoke Velocity Increase if the Whole Wing Were Blown.*
Under the slipstream model a fully blown wing would need a 54 percent velocity increase to supply the factor of 2.38.

$$
x_{whole} = \sqrt{2.38} - 1 = 0.544
\tag{10}
$$

*Equation 11, Bespoke Velocity Increase for the Blown Fraction.*
Under the slipstream model, with seventy percent of the span blown, the blown part needs a 73 percent velocity increase.

$$
x = \sqrt{1 + \frac{2.38 - 1}{0.70}} - 1 = 0.726
\tag{11}
$$

*Equation 12, Bespoke Slipstream Velocity Increment at the Stall Speed.*
The model's velocity increase applied at the 58 knot stall speed gives an increment of about 22 metres per second.

$$
\Delta V = x\,V_s = 0.726 \times 29.8 = 21.7
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Actuator Disc Thrust.**
Momentum theory gives the thrust of an ideal actuator disc from the disc area, the induced velocity and the free stream, with the far-wake increment twice the induced velocity.
[Momentum Theory][ref_momentum_theory]
[Glauert, The elements of aerofoil and airscrew theory][book_glauert]

$$
T = 2\rho A_h v_i \,(V_s + v_i), \qquad v_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta V
\tag{13}
$$

*Equation 14, Bespoke Ideal Power for the Whole Lift Factor.*
The ideal actuator disc power to produce the slipstream model's increment is about 139 kilowatts.

$$
P_i = T\,(V_s + v_i) = 139
\tag{14}
$$

*Equation 15, Bespoke Ideal Power Against Installed High-Lift Power.*
That ideal requirement is 92 percent of the 151 kilowatts installed, on the assumption that the propellers supply the whole factor of 2.38.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{P_i}{P_h} = \frac{139}{151} = 0.92
\tag{15}
$$

*Equation 16, Bespoke Real Power at an Assumed Propulsive Efficiency.*
At a propulsive efficiency of 75 percent that the article assumes, the power requirement exceeds the installed power.

$$
\frac{P_i}{\eta_{pr}} = \frac{139}{0.75} = 185 \;>\; P_h
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Stall Speed Scaled to the Mod II Mass.**
Scaling the production stall speed of 55 knots by the square root of the mass ratio reproduces the tabulated Mod II figure of 58 knots.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
V_{s,II} = V_{s,I}\sqrt{\frac{m_{II}}{m_{I}}} = 55\sqrt{\frac{1361}{1230}} = 57.9
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Maximum Lift Coefficient From a Stall Speed.**
The maximum lift coefficient follows from the stall speed, the mass, the wing area and the sea-level density.
[Lift Coefficient][ref_lift_coefficient]

$$
C_{L,max} = \frac{2\,m\,g}{\rho\,V_{s0}^{2}\,S}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Landing Lift Coefficients of Mod II, Mod IV and the Blown Wing.**
The tabulated landing stall speeds at 1,361 kilograms give maximum lift coefficients of 1.658, 2.496 and 3.954, the last agreeing with the design figure.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]
[Borer and Patterson][research_x57_high_lift_control_schedule]

$$
C_{L,II} = 1.658, \qquad C_{L,IV} = 2.496, \qquad C_{L,hl} = 3.954
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Division of the Lift Factor Between Flap and Propellers.**
The flapped small wing supplies a factor of 1.505 and the propellers the remaining 1.584, whose product recovers the 2.38.

$$
\frac{C_{L,IV}}{C_{L,II}} = 1.505, \qquad \frac{C_{L,hl}}{C_{L,IV}} = \left(\frac{73}{58}\right)^{2} = 1.584, \qquad 1.505 \times 1.584 = 2.384
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Design Lift Coefficient Against the Unblown Wing.**
The design lift coefficient of 4.35, sized with a ten percent margin, is 1.743 times the unblown Mod IV value.
[Borer and Patterson][research_x57_high_lift_control_schedule]

$$
\frac{C_{L,goal}}{C_{L,IV}} = \frac{4.35}{2.496} = 1.743
\tag{21}
$$

*Equation 22, Bespoke Velocity Increase for the Design Lift Factor.*
Put through the article's slipstream model, the design factor of 1.743 needs a velocity increase of 44 percent on the blown span.

$$
x = \sqrt{1 + \frac{1.743 - 1}{0.699}} - 1 = 0.436
\tag{22}
$$

*Equation 23, Bespoke Power for the Design Lift Factor.*
The ideal power for that increment is 66.6 kilowatts, and at the assumed 75 percent propulsive efficiency 88.7 kilowatts, below the installed power.

$$
P_i = 66.6, \qquad \frac{P_i}{\eta_{pr}} = \frac{66.6}{0.75} = 88.7 \;<\; P_h
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Design Shaft Power and Thrust of the High-Lift Propellers.**
Twelve propellers at the published design point of 10.7 kilowatts and 215 newtons give 128.4 kilowatts and 2,580 newtons.
[Borer and Patterson][research_x57_high_lift_control_schedule]

$$
P_s = 12 \times 10.7 = 128.4, \qquad T = 12 \times 215 = 2580
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Actuator Disc Evaluation of the Design Thrust.**
Treating the design thrust as twelve actuator discs of the published diameter gives the induced velocity, an ideal power of 99.5 kilowatts and an ideal to shaft power ratio of 0.775.
[Momentum Theory][ref_momentum_theory]

$$
v_i = 8.73, \qquad P_i = T\,(V_s + v_i) = 99.5, \qquad \frac{P_i}{P_s} = 0.775
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Design Slipstream Against the Model Requirement.*
The far-wake increment implied by the design thrust, 58 percent of the stall speed, exceeds the 44 percent that the article's slipstream model requires.

$$
\frac{2\,v_i}{V_s} = 0.585 \;>\; 0.436
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Ratio of Wetted Areas.**
The reported wetted areas, including the high-lift nacelles, fall by 18 percent.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{S_{w,1}}{S_{w,0}} = \frac{55.5}{67.8} = 0.819
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Induced Drag in Terms of Span.**
At given lift and speed the induced drag is set by the square of the span and the span efficiency, not by the aspect ratio.
[Lift-Induced Drag][ref_induced_drag]

$$
D_i = \frac{L^{2}}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}\,\pi\, b^{2} e}
\tag{28}
$$

**Equation 29, Ratio of Induced Drag From the Span Reduction.**
At equal lift, speed and span efficiency the shorter Mod III span raises the induced drag by 32 percent, as the report also concludes.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{D_{i,1}}{D_{i,0}} = \left(\frac{b_0}{b_1}\right)^{2}= \left(\frac{11.40}{9.94}\right)^{2} = 1.32
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Cruise Lift-to-Drag Gains of Mod III Over Mod II.**
The report's cruise lift-to-drag ratios give a gain of 40 percent without thrust and 53 percent with cruise thrust.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{13.3}{9.5} = 1.40, \qquad \frac{13.5}{8.8} = 1.53
\tag{30}
$$

**Equation 31, Effect of Thrust on Lift-to-Drag Ratio.**
Cruise thrust costs Mod II about seven percent of its lift-to-drag ratio and gains Mod III about two percent on the report's figures.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{8.8}{9.5} = 0.93, \qquad \frac{13.5}{13.3} = 1.02
\tag{31}
$$

**Equation 32, Aspect Ratio.**
The aspect ratio is the square of the span over the wing area, which allows a published set of span, area and aspect ratio to be checked.
[Aspect Ratio, Aeronautics][ref_aspect_ratio]

$$
AR = \frac{b^{2}}{S}
\tag{32}
$$

**Equation 33, Installed High-Lift and Cruise Motor Power.**
Twelve high-lift motors of 12.6 kilowatts give 151.2 kilowatts and two cruise motors of 72 kilowatts give 144.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
P_h = 12 \times 12.6 = 151.2, \qquad P_c = 2 \times 72 = 144
\tag{33}
$$

**Equation 34, High-Lift Power Against the Original Engines.**
The high-lift installation is three percent more powerful than the two 73.5 kilowatt piston engines it replaced.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{P_h}{P_0} = \frac{151.2}{147.0} = 1.03
\tag{34}
$$

**Equation 35, Propeller Advance Ratio.**
The advance ratio is the airspeed over the product of rotational speed and diameter.
[Propeller, Aeronautics][ref_propeller]

$$
J = \frac{V}{n\,d}
\tag{35}
$$

**Equation 36, Advance Ratios of the Cruise and High-Lift Propellers.**
At their design points the cruise propellers run at an advance ratio of 1.34 and the high-lift propellers at 0.68.

$$
J_{cruise} = 1.34, \qquad J_{lift} = 0.68
\tag{36}
$$

**Equation 37, Specific Power of the Cruise Motor and the Rotax Engine.**
The cruise motor with its propeller gives 1.36 kilowatts per kilogram against about 1.30 for the Rotax engine with its gearbox.
[X-57 Maxwell Overview, NASA][ref_nasa_x57]
[Rotax 912 ULS/S, BRP-Rotax][ref_rotax_912_uls]

$$
\frac{72}{53.1} = 1.36 \quad \text{against} \quad \frac{73.5}{56.6} = 1.30
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Cruise Motor Torque.**
Torque is power over angular speed, giving 255 newton metres at the 72 kilowatt peak rating and 2,700 revolutions per minute.
[Clarke et al][research_x57_x_57_traction_power_and_command]
[Clarke and Terry][research_x57_cruise_motor_inverter_failures]

$$
Q = \frac{P}{\Omega} = \frac{72\,000}{2\pi \times 2700/60} = 255
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Cruise Power Fraction at Reduced Speed.**
At full torque the cruise motor power falls in proportion to speed, to two thirds at 1,800 revolutions per minute.

$$
\frac{P_{1800}}{P_{2700}} = \frac{1800}{2700} = 0.67
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Specific Energy of the Battery Pack.**
The 47 kilowatt hours of effective energy in 390 kilograms of battery is 120 watt hours per kilogram.
[Hernandez Lugo et al. 2018][research_x57_battery_cell_to_system]

$$
e_b = \frac{E}{m} = \frac{47\times 10^{3}}{390} = 120\ \text{watt hours per kilogram}
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Module Voltage, Capacity and Energy.**
Sixteen cells in series of twenty in parallel give a module of 57.6 volts, 60 ampere hours and 3,456 watt hours.
[Clarke][research_x57_traction_power_system]
[Hernandez Lugo et al. 2018][research_x57_battery_cell_to_system]

$$
V_m = 16 \times 3.6 = 57.6, \qquad C_m = 20 \times 3.0 = 60, \qquad E_m = 57.6 \times 60 = 3456
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Nominal Pack Energy and Voltage Limits.**
Sixteen modules give 55.3 kilowatt hours, and 128 cells in series give a nominal 461 volts and a maximum of 538.
[Clarke][research_x57_traction_power_system]

$$
E_{nom} = 16 \times 3.456 = 55.3, \qquad V_{nom} = 128 \times 3.6 = 461, \qquad V_{max} = 128 \times 4.2 = 538
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Effective Fraction of Nominal Energy.**
The design counted 47 of the nominal 55.3 kilowatt hours as effective, a fraction of 0.85.

$$
\frac{E}{E_{nom}} = \frac{47}{55.3} = 0.85
\tag{43}
$$

**Equation 44, Specific Energy of the Fuel.**
A lower heating value of 43.5 megajoules per kilogram is about 12,100 watt hours per kilogram.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
e_f = \frac{43.5 \times 10^{6}}{3600} = 1.21 \times 10^{4}
\tag{44}
$$

**Equation 45, Ratio of Fuel to Battery Specific Energy.**
Fuel carries about a hundred times more energy per kilogram than this battery pack.

$$
\frac{e_f}{e_b} = 100
\tag{45}
$$

**Equation 46, Discharge Rate With Every Motor at Peak.**
Running all fourteen motors at their 295.2 kilowatt combined peak would draw 6.3 times the effective energy per hour.

$$
C_r = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{295.2}{47} = 6.3
\tag{46}
$$

**Equation 47, Endurance With Every Motor at Peak.**
At that combined peak the effective energy would last 0.159 hours, under ten minutes.

$$
t = \frac{E}{P} = \frac{47}{295.2} = 0.159
\tag{47}
$$

**Equation 48, Baseline Profile Energy Against Effective Energy.**
The baseline flight profile was predicted to need 98 percent of the effective energy.
[Hernandez Lugo et al. 2018][research_x57_battery_cell_to_system]

$$
\frac{E_{prof}}{E} = \frac{46.2}{47.0} = 0.98
\tag{48}
$$

**Equation 49, Endurance at the Continuous Requirement.**
At the 120 kilowatts the two subsystems had to sustain continuously, the effective energy lasts 0.39 hours.
[Hernandez Lugo et al. 2018][research_x57_battery_cell_to_system]

$$
t = \frac{E}{P} = \frac{47}{120} = 0.39
\tag{49}
$$

**Equation 50, Pack Current at Nominal and Minimum Voltage.**
At 60 kilowatts the current is 130 amperes at the 461 volt nominal and 176 at the 340 volt landing floor.
[Clarke et al][research_x57_x_57_traction_power_and_command]

$$
I = \frac{P}{V_b}, \qquad \frac{60\,000}{461} = 130, \qquad \frac{60\,000}{340} = 176
\tag{50}
$$

**Equation 51, Net Energy Disadvantage Per Kilogram.**
The hundredfold specific energy deficit divided by the threefold drivetrain efficiency advantage on the report's figures leaves the battery thirty-three times worse off per kilogram.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{e_f\,\eta_p}{e_b\,\eta_e} = \frac{100 \times 0.30}{0.90} = 33
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Decomposition of the Energy Goal.**
The fivefold energy goal is the efficiency gain from 28 to 92 percent multiplied by a factor of 1.5 from the configuration.
[Borer][research_x57_flight_performance_estimates]

$$
\frac{0.92}{0.28} \times 1.5 = 3.29 \times 1.5 = 4.9
\tag{52}
$$

*Equation 53, Bespoke Combined Energy Reduction of Mod III.*
Multiplying the report's Mod II energy ratios by the Mod III cruise lift-to-drag gain combines estimates made at different conditions, an inference the article draws and the report does not state.

$$
2.6 \times 1.53 = 4.0, \qquad 2.9 \times 1.53 = 4.4
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Electric Aircraft Range.**
The steady cruise range of an electric aircraft is the stored energy times the drivetrain and propulsive efficiencies over the weight, times the lift-to-drag ratio.
[Range, Aeronautics][ref_breguet]
[Lift-to-Drag Ratio][ref_lift_to_drag]

$$
R = \frac{E\,\eta_e\,\eta_{pr}}{m\,g}\;\frac{L}{D}
\tag{54}
$$

*Equation 55, Bespoke Upper Bound on Mod II and Mod III Range.*
Spending all 47 kilowatt hours at the cruise point with a propulsive efficiency of 75 percent that the article assumes gives upper bounds of 75 and 116 kilometres.

$$
R_{II} = 75, \qquad R_{III} = 116
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Cruise Motor Controller Switching Voltage and Current.**
The cruise motor controller switched at the 538 volt bus maximum and 200 amperes peak per phase.
[Clarke and Terry][research_x57_cruise_motor_inverter_failures]

$$
V_{dc} = 538, \qquad I_{pk} = 200
\tag{56}
$$

**Equation 57, Controller Heat Limit and Throughput.**
At 97 percent efficiency the 330 watt heat limit corresponds to 11 kilowatts of throughput.
[Clarke et al][research_x57_x_57_traction_power_and_command]

$$
P_{loss} = (1 - \eta_c)\,P, \qquad \frac{330}{0.03} = 11\,000
\tag{57}
$$

### Notation

- $S_1$, the Mod III wing area, with $S_0$ the original wing area
- $W/S$, the wing loading
- $C_L$, the lift coefficient
- $C_{L,max}$, the maximum lift coefficient
- $V_s$, the stall speed
- $q_w$, the dynamic pressure over the blown wing
- $\Delta V$, the slipstream velocity increment
- $f$, the fraction of the span in a slipstream
- $d$, the propeller diameter
- $b_1$, the Mod III span, with $b_0$ the original span
- $A_h$, the total disc area of the high-lift propellers
- $x$, the fractional velocity increase over the blown span
- $v_i$, the induced velocity at the disc
- $P_i$, the ideal induced power
- $P_h$, the installed high-lift motor power
- $\eta_{pr}$, the propulsive efficiency
- $C_{L,hl}$, the maximum lift coefficient with the high-lift propellers running
- $C_{L,goal}$, the design maximum lift coefficient
- $P_s$, the design shaft power of the high-lift propellers
- $S_{w,1}$, the Mod III wetted area, with $S_{w,0}$ the original
- $D_i$, the induced drag
- $e$, the span efficiency
- $AR$, the wing aspect ratio
- $P_c$, the installed cruise motor power
- $J$, the propeller advance ratio
- $Q$, the motor torque
- $\Omega$, the angular speed of the motor
- $e_b$, the specific energy of the battery pack
- $e_f$, the specific energy of the fuel
- $E_{nom}$, the nominal pack energy
- $C_r$, the discharge rate as a multiple of capacity per hour
- $E_{prof}$, the energy predicted for the baseline flight profile
- $V_b$, the pack voltage
- $\eta_e$, the electric drivetrain efficiency, with $\eta_p$ the piston engine efficiency
- $\eta_c$, the motor controller efficiency
- $P_{loss}$, the heat dissipated in the controller
